note: Rebuilt on every run of .github/workflows/daily-creator-pull.yml from the hooks harvested that day. Spyglass HOOK/USP aggregation returns empty for these creators because it is tuned to paid campaigns, so the patterns are read off the organic hooks themselves. Every quote is verified against a harvested hook before it is written.

patterns.label: opens as a question to an expert
patterns.description: The first line is the interviewer's question, so the viewer arrives mid-conversation and the answer is obviously seconds away. Borrowed authority does the work: someone else is on the hook to deliver.

examples.creator: Sean Pan
examples.quote: Does it matter if you intend to have like housemates and stuff like that?

examples.creator: Michael Llanas
examples.quote: I really want to deep dive into owner financing because I know that's what you specialize in

examples.creator: Ravi Sharma
examples.quote: So how do you adapt post budget around building wealth with property?

examples.creator: Jerry Norton
examples.quote: What would a package deal look like if I bought this and Iowa?

patterns.label: starts mid-sentence, already talking
patterns.description: The clip begins as if the viewer walked in late — a fragment, a connective word, an unfinished phrase. The missing beginning creates the pull, and the informality reads as unedited and real rather than scripted.

examples.creator: Jerry Norton
examples.quote: Okay, so the next thing I need to talk about some earnest money, man,

examples.creator: Logan Fullmer
examples.quote: Why do I care?

examples.creator: Michael Llanas
examples.quote: The calling listings that have been on the market for a long time.

patterns.label: names a rule or program by name
patterns.description: The hook drops the official name of a piece of legislation or a program the viewer probably cannot define, creating an information gap that feels urgent because it is already law or already proposed. The specificity signals insider knowledge rather than opinion.

examples.creator: Scott Betley
examples.quote: Hey Kyle, have you heard about the MOVE Act that Congress just proposed that can help homeowners keep their lower interest rates?

examples.creator: Scott Kuru
examples.quote: If the government's new SMSF property rules have got you thinking, "Fine, I can't borrow for residential anymore. I'll just buy commercial."

patterns.label: opens with an if-clause that filters
patterns.description: A conditional opening sorts the audience in the first three words, so anyone who fits feels personally addressed and cannot scroll. The payoff is attached directly to the condition, so the instruction arrives inside the hook itself.

examples.creator: Theoni Rapo
examples.quote: If the house that you like on Zillow is still on the market, ask for a seller credit.

examples.creator: Scott Kuru
examples.quote: If you own property in Australia, you need to understand just how much the tax office can actually see about you,

patterns.label: leads with the exact dollar number
patterns.description: The opening line puts a hard, oddly specific figure on the table before any teaching happens, so the claim reads as a receipt rather than a promise. The number also implies the rest of the video explains how it happened.

examples.creator: Sean Pan
examples.quote: I bought this 4plex for $250,000 and this is how much I make from it.

examples.creator: Jack Henderson
examples.quote: We just finished building it, and we made a sneaky, "one and a half million bucks" along the way.

patterns.label: claims a number one or best
patterns.description: The hook stakes a superlative — the best place, the number one property — which is both instantly checkable and instantly arguable, so viewers stay either to verify or to disagree.

examples.creator: Jeremy Werden
examples.quote: Five years ago, we turned this into North Carolina's number one Airbnb.

examples.creator: Logan Fullmer
examples.quote: One of the best places in all the land to buy distressed property is right here, your county courthouse.

patterns.label: points at something in frame
patterns.description: A short deictic line — see this, this is — forces the eye to the visual and makes the viewer look for what is unusual about it. It works because the sentence is incomplete without the image.

examples.creator: Jack Henderson
examples.quote: You see this little house here?

examples.creator: Erick Brice
examples.quote: This is your house This is your house Hey

patterns.label: names what everyone is panicking about
patterns.description: The hook opens on a collective emotional state — freaking out, scared, asking if it is dead — which validates the feeling before correcting it. The viewer stays because their own worry has just been said out loud.

examples.creator: Ravi Sharma
examples.quote: Prices are falling and people are freaking out

examples.creator: Michael Llanas
examples.quote: Most up to investors when they're looking at their first up to deal, everyone's always scared of the due on sale clause.

patterns.label: reports a real deal in progress
patterns.description: The line announces something that just happened or is happening right now on an actual property, with names and places attached. It earns attention as documentary access rather than instruction.

examples.creator: Jerry Norton
examples.quote: So Jared and I are out here at a house in Maryville that Jared made an offer on.

examples.creator: Jack Henderson
examples.quote: Another council approval has just come through for one of our Henderson equity factory deals.

patterns.label: drops you into a hypothetical scene
patterns.description: The hook assigns the viewer a role or a future — your age, your night — in the second person, so they are inside the story before they know what it is about. Curiosity about their own assigned situation carries the next beat.

examples.creator: Erick Brice
examples.quote: You're 20 years old.

examples.creator: Emeline SIRON - Experte investissement immobilier
examples.quote: Cette nuit, tu vas gagner de l'argent en dormant.

patterns.label: opens by forbidding something (single example)
patterns.description: A flat prohibition or denial of a thing the viewer assumes is fine, with the reason deliberately withheld behind a word like unless. The negative command is harder to ignore than advice because it implies a mistake already in motion.

examples.creator: Jeremy Werden
examples.quote: Do not buy a lakefront or beachfront property unless you consider this.
